paragraphs.text: Faletra et al. (2014) noted that Stickler syndrome is clinically variable and genetically heterogeneous, with ophthalmic, articular, orofacial, and auditory manifestations. It shows both autosomal dominant inheritance (COL2A1, COL11A1, COL11A2) and autosomal recessive inheritance (COL9A1, COL9A2). Stickler syndrome type VI is the autosomal recessive form caused by loss-of-function mutations in the COL9A3 gene. Its consistent features are moderate-to-profound progressive sensorineural hearing loss and moderate-to-high myopia with vitreoretinal degeneration, and skeletal involvement varies (Rad et al., 2022).

paragraphs.text: Hanson-Kahn et al. (2018) reported a boy with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome whose parents, from India, were third cousins. He failed his newborn hearing screen. At 5 months, testing showed moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss on the right and severe loss on the left, and the hearing loss remained stable. Temporal bone CT showed mild enlargement of the vestibular aqueducts. He had no myopia at 5 months but had high myopia by 2 years (-6.75 OD, -8 OS), which progressed to -10.75 OD and -11.25 OS by 12 years. No vitreous abnormalities were noted. He had femoral and tibial bowing at birth. Radiographs at age 6 years showed slightly flattened proximal femoral epiphyses, flattened acetabula, irregular medial distal femoral epiphyses, and mild platyspondyly with irregular vertebral endplates. Growth and intelligence were normal, and he had neither cleft palate nor pes planus. He had midfacial hypoplasia, and autoimmune hypothyroidism was diagnosed at 10 years.

paragraphs.text: Markova et al. (2021) described a Russian boy with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome whose parents were healthy and nonconsanguineous. At 1 month he had hip dysplasia and bilaterally absent ossification centers. Congenital high bilateral myopia was noted at 3 months, and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss grade 3-4 was diagnosed at 11 months. Ophthalmic findings included peripheral pigment rearrangement, multiple vitreous floaters, a preretinal membrane, and congenital progressive high myopia. The ERG was normal. Radiographs at 1 and 3 years showed mild spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia with platyspondyly, kyphosis, sacral spina bifida occulta, flattened irregular femoral heads, coxa valga, and flattened distal femoral epiphyses. When examined at 2 years 5 months, he had valgus knee deformity and waddling gait. From age 3 years he had fatigability and pain in the lower limb joints, which the authors took to indicate early-onset arthropathy. His height was normal. He had a flattened nasal bridge, small nose, mild midface hypoplasia, and high palate, without cleft palate. The authors concluded that his phenotype was more severe than in previously reported COL9A3 patients, with early-onset arthropathy and vitreoretinal degeneration.

The patient had no arthritis but had a history of cataract and retinal detachment. She had first been diagnosed with nonsyndromic hearing loss, and the cataract and retinal detachment were recognized only on re-evaluation after the genetic diagnosis. The authors classified her as having a very mild type of Stickler syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Rad et al. (2022) described 5 patients from 3 unrelated consanguineous Iranian families. The proband of family 1 was a 28-year-old woman, the only affected child of first-cousin parents. She had high myopia in both eyes, vitreoretinal degeneration with empty vitreous, multiple lattice degenerations, retinal pigmentary changes, and severe progressive sensorineural hearing loss. Skull x-ray showed unilateral absence of the frontal sinus. Her joints and bones were normal on examination, but she complained of knee pain. She lacked typical Stickler craniofacial features, including midface hypoplasia, cleft palate, micrognathia, depressed nasal bridge, and anteverted nares. Her height was 157 cm (-0.8 SD).

paragraphs.text: Goldstein et al. (2010) studied oculoskeletal dysplasia (OSD), which segregates as an autosomal recessive trait in Labrador retriever dogs (locus drd1) and Samoyed dogs (locus drd2). Affected pups could be recognized from about 4 to 6 weeks of age by excessive doming of the cranium, a pronounced facial stop, exotropic strabismus, and short-limbed dwarfism with forelimb curvature and varus/valgus deformity. Eye examination showed radial cortical equatorial cataracts, vitreal liquefaction, and frequent complete retinal detachment. The authors noted that the phenotype resembles human arthro-ophthalmopathies such as Stickler syndrome. Dogs heterozygous at either locus had a normal skeleton but could show a mild eye phenotype of retinal folds and vitreal strands. Among Labrador-derived litters, 14 of 34 obligate heterozygotes had retinal folds. However, retinal folds were not linked to the COL9A3 locus, and 18 Labradors with retinal folds were wildtype at that locus. The authors suggested a possible semidominant mechanism in which haploinsufficiency affects the vitreous but not cartilage.

paragraphs.text: In 8 colony families derived from Labrador retrievers, Goldstein et al. (2010) mapped the drd1 locus to the telomeric end of canine chromosome 24 (maximum lod score 3.589 with marker FH2079), making COL9A3 a positional candidate gene. Affected dogs were homozygous for a 1-bp insertion (G) in exon 1 of COL9A3 that causes a frameshift and a premature stop codon after 48 codons, affecting the COL3 domain. The mutation cosegregated with the disease (lod score 25.889 at theta 0.0): all affected dogs were homozygous and all obligate carriers were heterozygous. Among 59 unrelated Labradors and 19 Labradors with retinal folds, 1 dog was homozygous, and that dog also had short-limbed dwarfism. The allele frequency was estimated at about 1%, and 78 dogs from 21 other breeds were wildtype. On Northern blots, COL9A3 mRNA (about 3.0 kb) was not detectable in retina from an affected dog, whereas COL9A2 was still expressed. Because the promoter was not mutated, the authors suggested that nonsense-mediated decay was the likely mechanism. In drd2-affected Samoyeds, the authors identified a homozygous 1,267-bp deletion at the 5-prime end of COL9A2 that removes exon 1. This deletion cosegregated with the disease (lod score 23.179), and COL9A2 mRNA was absent from affected retina. The authors stated that the canine diseases provide valuable models for the recessive form of Stickler syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Stavinohova et al. (2019) described oculoskeletal dysplasia in 7 Northern Inuit Dogs from 3 related litters in the UK. All affected dogs had short-limbed (disproportionate) dwarfism and angular limb deformities, together with a variable combination of macroglobus, cataracts, lens coloboma, microphakia, and vitreopathy. Five dogs had retinal detachment. In most dogs the ocular lesions progressed to advanced cataract, lens-induced uveitis, posterior lens subluxation, secondary glaucoma, and blindness. Pedigree analysis indicated autosomal recessive inheritance. Histopathology of an enucleated globe showed a hydrophthalmic globe with lens luxation, cortical cataract, vitreal syneresis, and chronic rhegmatogenous retinal detachment without retinal dysplasia (rosettes), and a presumptive diagnosis of vitreoretinopathy was made. Unlike affected Labrador retrievers, affected Northern Inuit Dogs lacked retinal dysplasia, and heterozygous dogs were free of ocular defects.

paragraphs.text: After excluding the known drd1 and drd2 variants, Stavinohova et al. (2019) performed whole genome sequencing of 2 affected Northern Inuit Dogs and screened 9 candidate genes. They identified a homozygous nonsense variant in exon 14 of COL9A3 (c.700C-T, R234X), predicted to truncate the protein by 451 amino acids. All 7 affected dogs were homozygous. Of 116 unaffected Northern Inuit Dogs, 31 were heterozygous and 85 were homozygous wildtype (p = 1.4 x 10(-11)), consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance with complete penetrance. All 1,109 dogs of other breeds were homozygous wildtype, and the allele frequency in Northern Inuit Dogs was 0.08. Retinal COL9A3 mRNA was not reduced in an affected dog, suggesting that nonsense-mediated decay may not contribute, although the results were inconclusive.
